title: The Bill

post.author: u/bay_light_laimonas
post.title: I'm the night attendant at a 24-hour car wash. At midnight the cloud bill came: $25,132.03 for September. We took $19,400. Then I looked up at the cameras.

blocks.text: I'm Laimonas, night attendant at the Rinsemoor Car Wash: 4 bays, open all hours, me in the kiosk from 22:00 to 06:00. Mrs Oluwole, the owner, does the paperwork on Thursday mornings. A camera in each bay's roof films every car, in case a customer says we scratched it.

A video is a fast run of still pictures, 30 a second on ours. Each picture is called a frame. Our frames go to the cloud: computers we rent from a big company, the cloud company, paying only for what we use.

There, each frame goes through three steps. Each step is a small program, a list of instructions for a computer, that the cloud company starts for one job and stops straight after. That kind of program is called a serverless function.

When a step stops, its memory is wiped: the computer's short-term working space, like a whiteboard cleaned after every job. So the steps pass the frame through storage, the cloud company's long-term shelf.

A frame's trip, in order. First, step 1 saves the frame to storage: a storage write. Second, step 2 reads it back, a storage read, and looks for a car. Third, step 3 reads it again and files it under its bay and time.

The cloud company starts each step by passing it the job: a hand-off, three per frame. It prices each kind per million, like gravel per tonne: writes $5, reads $0.40, hand-offs $25. So one frame, with 1 write, 2 reads and 3 hand-offs, costs $80.80 per million frames.

The bill is added up in steps. At midnight on the month's last day, the cloud company counts each kind, multiplies each count by its price per million, and adds the lines. It emails the bill to our shop inbox on the kiosk computer, and I print it for Mrs Oluwole's Thursday folder.
Tonight was Wednesday 30 September. At 00:05, Thursday now, I opened September's. Each line: what was counted, how many, the price per million, the cost.

blocks.title: Your cloud bill, September 2026. Sent Thursday 1 October, 00:00.
items: Hand-offs between steps: 933,120,000 at $25.00 per million: $23,328.00
Storage space: on your yearly plan, paid in January: $0.00

blocks.text: The wash took $19,400 in September. The cloud took $25,132.03: $20.94 for each of our 1,200 washes. August: $0.44 a wash, for the same 1,200.

311,040,000 writes. On the till roll: 4 bays, 30 frames a second, 86,400 seconds a day, 30 days. Every second of September, car or no car. I looked up through the kiosk window. Over each empty bay, a camera's red recording light was on.
Four cameras filming nothing, and something counting every frame.

Their settings page explained it. Updates to their built-in software, the firmware, install themselves at 00:00 on the 1st of a month when the maker sends one: download, install, restart. Tuesday 1 September's put every setting back to the maker's default: "record when a car is in the bay" became "always record", from that second.

blocks.label: bays_around_midnight.png

diagram.aria: Wednesday 30 September 23:50 to Thursday 1 October 00:10. All four cameras record the whole 20 minutes (red). No car is in any bay the whole time. September's bill is still open until 00:00, when it closes and is emailed. Markers: 00:00 the bill is sent; 00:05 Laimonas reads it.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the cameras' settings page and the bill email, Wednesday 30 September 23:50 to Thursday 1 October 00:10. Red is the four cameras recording. No car came in those 20 minutes, yet the cameras sent 4 x 30 x 1,200 = 144,000 frames: $11.64 at $80.80 per million.

blocks.text: Before, the cameras recorded only during washes, 3 minutes each: 6,480,000 frames a month, $523.58. The saved frames are our footage, kept 30 days for claims. Nobody set a budget alarm, which works in two steps: each day the cloud company adds up the month's spending so far, and once it passes an amount you chose, it emails you. The red lights are four metres up; nobody looks.
Mrs Oluwole reads her folder at 08:00. What should she change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Don't look at the total yet. Which line is biggest, and what sets how many of those there are: the cars, or something else? You're paying per request, each time a small thing happens, so the count is the whole bill. Then ask who owns each line: whose job is it to notice when one grows 48 times?

replies.author: u/bay_light_laimonas
replies.text: Hand-offs: $23,328.00 of it. The count follows the cameras' frames, not the cars. And nobody owns any line. A contractor built the steps two years ago and has gone; Mrs Oluwole pays the bill by card and files it.

comments.author: u/pay_per_use_boleslaw
comments.text: Serverless means you only pay for what you use: no computers sitting idle, nothing wasted. So the design can't be the problem. At 311 million frames you're a big customer now, and big customers get a volume discount, a lower price per million for buying a lot. Ring the cloud company in the morning and ask.

replies.author: u/bay_light_laimonas
replies.text: Mrs Oluwole would rather make a phone call than rebuild anything.

comments.author: u/clear_the_shelf_juhani
comments.text: 311 million frames landing on a shelf every month is the mess. Keep the footage 7 days instead of 30 and the pile stops growing.

replies.author: u/bay_light_laimonas
replies.text: That's one box on the kiosk computer. I could change it tonight.

reply.prompt: Mrs Oluwole reads the folder at 08:00 on Thursday. What should she change first? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Ask the cloud company for a volume discount on the storage writes and the hand-offs.
options.verdict: A lower price on the same count
options.part2: At 09:00 on Thursday Mrs Oluwole rang the cloud company. A salesman offered 15% off every line in return for a promise of the same spending for a year, and she signed. In the sim, replaying September with 15% off: $21,362.23, $17.80 a wash, still more than the $19,400 the wash took. The cameras kept recording every second, because nothing about them had changed, and October has 31 days. She now owes a year of it.
options.senior: A discount changes the price per million, never the count, and the count is what went wrong: 48 times the frames since one camera setting changed. Even 15% off leaves the bill above the takings. Worse, a discount bought with a promise to keep spending locks the waste in for a year. Find what sets the count first; negotiate prices only for spending you have decided to keep.

options.text: Run one small program per bay that keeps frames in memory and saves 2 photos a wash.
options.part2: On Thursday Mrs Oluwole had the contractor back. By Monday 5 October each bay had one small program running all the time on a small rented computer in the cloud, $12 a month each in this story's prices. The camera sends it every frame; the program keeps only the last few seconds in memory, and when the bay's car sensor says a wash has started or ended, it saves that frame as a photo: 2 a wash. In the sim, replaying September with one program per bay: 2,400 photos, $0.01 of storage writes, $48.00 for the four programs, $48.01 in all, $0.04 a wash, whether the cameras record always or only with a car in the bay. She set a budget alarm at $100, made herself the owner of every line, and added cost per wash to her Thursday sheet. The red lights still burn all night. They cost nothing now.
options.senior: When work arrives as a steady stream, 30 frames a second all night, paying per request multiplies a tiny price by a huge count. A program that stays on costs the same whatever passes through it, and keeping frames in memory removes the storage writes, the reads and the hand-offs together. Save only what the business needs, 2 photos a wash, so the count follows washes, not seconds. Then watch the number that matters, cost per wash, with a budget alarm and a named owner for each line, so the next surprise shows in a day, not a month.

options.text: Set the cameras back to record only when a car is in the bay, and add a budget alarm.
options.verdict: Trade-off: cheap again, one reset away
options.part2: From the kiosk computer I set all four cameras back to record when a car is in the bay, and Mrs Oluwole set a budget alarm at $600. In the sim, replaying September that way: 6,480,000 frames, $523.58, $0.44 a wash, and the alarm never fires. With the alarm on and the cameras left on always record, it fires on Tuesday 1 September, after one day's $837.73. On Sunday 1 November at 00:00 the cameras' next update reset the setting again. The alarm emailed on Sunday, and Mrs Oluwole set it back on Monday morning: in the sim, two days of always record cost $1,675.47.
options.senior: This is an honest fix: it brings the count back in line with the washes, and the alarm turns a month-long surprise into a day-long one. But the design still pays per frame, so the bill still rises and falls with a camera setting that someone else's update can reset, and every extra second of recording costs three hand-offs. It is a sound first move tonight; the steps that bill by the frame are still the thing to change.

options.text: Delete old footage sooner, so the stored frames stop piling up month after month.
options.part2: I changed the footage box from 30 days to 7 that night. In the sim, replaying September with 7 days kept: the September frames still in storage at the month's end fall from 311,040,000 to 72,576,000, and the bill is $25,132.03, to the cent. The space was on the yearly plan all along, and deleting is free in this story's price list. The bill counts writes, reads and hand-offs, and the cameras went on making them every second.
options.senior: Storage space is not what this bill charges for; requests are. Every frame is written once and read twice whether it is kept 7 days or 30, so keeping less changes the size of the pile and nothing on the bill. Before cutting a cost, read which line it sits on and what drives that line's count.

sim.title: Replay September's cloud bill at the Rinsemoor
sim.lede: You're Mrs Oluwole on Thursday morning, replaying September 2026 from 00:00 on Tuesday 1 September, a day at a time, to the bill at midnight on Wednesday 30 September. As given data: 4 bays, each camera 30 frames a second, 86,400 seconds a day, 30 days; 1,200 washes of 3 minutes, 40 a day; takings $19,400. Story prices per million: storage writes $5, storage reads $0.40, hand-offs $25. With the three steps, each frame is 1 write, 2 reads and 3 hand-offs. One program per bay costs $12 a month and saves 2 photos a wash. The volume discount on offer is 15%. Footage is kept 30 days; its space is on a yearly plan, and deleting is free. Set the recording, the design, a budget alarm, the discount and the days kept, then step a day or play to 30 September.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built: 311,040,000 frames, $25,132.03, $20.94 a wash, no alarm. Set recording to only with a car in the bay: 6,480,000 frames, $523.58, $0.44 a wash. Switch to one program per bay: 2,400 photos, $48.01, $0.04 a wash, with either recording setting. Take the 15% discount: $21,362.23. Keep footage 7 days: fewer frames kept, the same $25,132.03. Set the budget alarm at $600 with always record: it fires on Tuesday 1 September; at $5,000, on Sunday 6 September.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at the wash broke. In the cloud company's building, three small steps woke for every frame the cameras sent, and the bill counts those wakings, not cars. A firmware update on 1 September made the cameras send every second, 48 times the frames, and nobody owned the bill or had set an alarm to notice before the month closed.

steps.title: A frame's trip, and what each part of it costs.
steps.text: Every frame makes the same trip through the cloud company's building. First, the camera sends it, and a hand-off starts step 1 ($25 per million). Second, step 1 saves the frame to storage, a storage write ($5 per million), because a step's memory is wiped when it stops. Third, a hand-off starts step 2, which reads the frame back ($0.40 per million) and looks for a car. Fourth, a hand-off starts step 3, which reads it again and files it. That is 1 write, 2 reads and 3 hand-offs: $80.80 per million frames. What can go wrong at every step is the same thing: each piece is a fraction of a cent, so nobody notices it, and the number of frames is chosen by the camera, not by anyone who pays.

steps.title: How the bill is built: count times price, line by line.
steps.text: A request is one ask of the cloud company: one write, one read or one hand-off. The bill is built in three steps. First, the cloud company counts each kind of request for the month. Second, it multiplies each count by its price per million. Third, it adds the lines. September: 311,040,000 writes, $1,555.20; 622,080,000 reads, $248.83; 933,120,000 hand-offs, $23,328.00; total $25,132.03. The hand-offs alone are about 93% of it. Storage space is not on it at all: the space sits on a yearly plan, and deleting is free in this story's prices. So the bill is set by how many times things happen, not by how much is kept. Treating that bill as part of the design, with numbers someone watches and owns, is called FinOps.

steps.title: One setting set the count, and nothing was watching it.
steps.text: Always record: 4 bays x 30 frames a second x 86,400 seconds x 30 days = 311,040,000 frames, from 00:00 on Tuesday 1 September, when the firmware update put the setting back to its default. Record when a car is in the bay: 1,200 washes x 3 minutes x 60 seconds x 30 frames = 6,480,000 frames, $523.58, exactly 48 times fewer. For two years the count followed the cars, so the bill followed the business. The update cut that link, and three things that could have caught it were missing. No budget alarm: nothing compared the spending with what was expected until the month closed. No cost per wash: it went from $0.44 to $20.94, more than a wash takes on average, and nobody was looking at that number. No owner: the contractor had gone, Mrs Oluwole paid by card, and the bill reached a folder, not a person who would ask why.

steps.title: The fix: pay for a program that stays on, not for every frame.
steps.text: One small program per bay runs all the time on a small rented computer, $12 a month each in this story. First, the camera sends it every frame. Second, it keeps the last few seconds in memory, which costs nothing per frame. Third, when the bay's car sensor says a wash has started or ended, it saves that moment's frame as a photo: one storage write. Fourth, it lets the rest go. September replayed: 2,400 photos, $0.01, plus $48.00 for the four programs: $48.01, $0.04 a wash, whatever the cameras' setting. This is the move Prime Video made in 2023 (below). Then the habits, which is what designing with cost in mind means: a budget alarm at $100, cost per wash on Mrs Oluwole's Thursday sheet, and one named owner for every line of the bill, who is told when it moves. Serverless is usually cheaper when work comes in bursts with long gaps; a steady stream, 30 frames a second all night, is usually cheaper on something that stays on.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail, and the walk into the other building.
steps.text: A volume discount lowers the price, not the count: 15% off is still $21,362.23, more than the $19,400 the wash took. Deleting footage sooner changes what is kept, not what is counted: the bill stays $25,132.03. Moving to a cheaper region, the cloud company's computers in another part of the world, might shave the price per million, but the 933,120,000 hand-offs still happen. Setting the cameras back to record only with a car is honest and quick, $523.58 a month, but the bill still rises and falls with a camera setting that an update can reset. On Thursday morning Laimonas stayed past his shift and sat with Mrs Oluwole at the kiosk computer. She opened the cloud company's billing page for the first time, and they walked down it line by line, into the building where the night began: three small steps, waking 311 million times for four empty bays.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for one bay. The bay camera sends 30 frames a second to the bay program, which keeps them in memory and costs $12 a month. The bay's car sensor tells the program when a wash starts and ends. The program saves 2 photos a wash to storage. Storage writes go on the monthly bill, $48.01 for September with $0.04 a wash. The bill's spending so far feeds a budget alarm that emails Mrs Oluwole at $100.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for one bay. The camera's frames go to one program that stays on and keeps them in memory, so no frame is written, read or handed off. Only when the car sensor marks a wash's start or end does the program save a photo: 2 a wash, 2,400 in September. The bill becomes $48.01, $0.04 a wash, and a budget alarm at $100 watches the spending so far.

fix.title: The fix: one program per bay, cost per wash, a budget alarm and an owner for every line
fix.text: Replace the three per-frame steps with one small program per bay that stays on, keeps frames in memory and saves only the before and after photos of each wash, so the count of paid requests follows the washes, not the seconds. Write down the expected cost per wash before any change goes live, and put the real one on the weekly sheet. Set a budget alarm a little above the expected month. Give every line of the bill a named owner who is told when it moves. And when a camera, a setting or an update can change how often something runs, ask what that does to the bill.

limits: The four programs cost $48.00 a month whether the bays are busy or empty, and each one is now something to keep running: if a program stops, that bay saves no photos until someone restarts it, so it needs a check that it is alive. On a very quiet month, the per-frame steps would have cost less.

A budget alarm is late by design. The guide to AWS Budgets, the budget alarm of AWS (Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud company), says its budget figures are updated up to three times a day, and that a notification can come after the charge, so "fires on 1 September" means some hours into the day, not at the first frame.
Cost per wash only helps if someone reads it. Mrs Oluwole's sheet is weekly; a change that doubles the bill on a Friday still runs for days before Thursday.

explain.seniorTake: Cost is a property of the design, like speed or safety, and on a cloud bill it is almost always a count times a price. Before building, write the count down in business terms: per wash, per order, per user. Ask what sets that count, and who could change it without telling you: a camera, a retry setting, a partner's update. Per-request services are a fine choice for work that comes in bursts; for a steady stream, something that stays on is usually cheaper, and moving data in memory instead of through storage removes whole lines of the bill. Then make the bill visible while it grows, not after: a budget alarm, a cost per unit someone reads each week, and an owner for every line. A discount is the last lever, not the first.

realWorld.title: Prime Video, 2023: the two most expensive parts
realWorld.text: Marcin Kolny's post describes a tool that checks Prime Video's live streams for faults, built first from serverless pieces on AWS (Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud company). "The two most expensive operations in terms of cost were the orchestration workflow and when data passed between distributed components." Orchestration is the part that hands work from step to step: the Rinsemoor's hand-offs.

realWorld.title: Prime Video: billed per state transition
realWorld.text: "Our service performed multiple state transitions for every second of the stream, so we quickly reached account limits." And: "Besides that, AWS Step Functions charges users per state transition." A state transition is AWS's name for one move from step to step.

realWorld.title: Prime Video: frames through storage
realWorld.text: "To reduce computationally expensive video conversion jobs, we built a microservice that splits videos into frames and temporarily uploads images to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket." The detectors then read them back, and "However, the high number of Tier-1 calls to the S3 bucket was expensive." A bucket is a named container for files in storage.

realWorld.title: What Tier-1 means on an S3 bill
realWorld.text: AWS's guide to S3 billing codes describes Requests-Tier1 as "The number of PUT, COPY, or POST requests for S3 Standard, RRS, and tags, plus LIST requests for all buckets and objects", and Requests-Tier2 as "The number of GET and all other non-Tier1 requests". PUT is a write and GET a read: Prime Video's expensive calls were mostly the story's storage writes.

realWorld.title: Prime Video: one process, frames in memory
realWorld.text: "We realized that distributed approach wasn’t bringing a lot of benefits in our specific use case, so we packed all of the components into a single process." Then: "This eliminated the need for the S3 bucket as the intermediate storage for video frames because our data transfer now happened in the memory."

realWorld.title: Prime Video: over 90% cheaper, case by case
realWorld.text: "Moving our service to a monolith reduced our infrastructure cost by over 90%." A monolith is one program doing all the parts. The post does not say serverless is wrong: "Microservices and serverless components are tools that do work at high scale, but whether to use them over monolith has to be made on a case-by-case basis."

realWorld.title: The story's hand-off price: AWS Step Functions
realWorld.text: AWS's pricing page says: "You are charged based on the number of state transitions required to execute your application." Its worked example says: "The price per state transition in US East (N. Virginia) is $0.000025 and the Free Tier provides 4,000 state transitions per month." That is $25 per million, the story's hand-off price.

realWorld.title: The story's write and read prices: Amazon S3
realWorld.text: S3's pricing page, as read, says in one example: "S3 GET requests from the S3 Standard storage class cost $0.0004 per 1,000 requests." That is $0.40 per million, the story's read price. The S3 Standard table for writes did not show in the page as read; its S3 Tables example says "S3 Tables - Standard PUT request price is $0.005 per 1,000 requests", $5 per million, so the story's write price is a story price. And: "DELETE and CANCEL requests are free."

realWorld.title: AWS Budgets: an alarm, a little late
realWorld.text: AWS's guide: "You can use AWS Budgets to track and take action on your AWS costs and usage." Notifications can go "to an email address". But: "AWS Budgets information is updated up to three times a day." And: "There can be a delay between when you incur a charge and when you receive a notification from AWS Budgets for the charge."

realWorld.title: The FinOps Foundation: everyone owns their cost
realWorld.text: The FinOps Foundation calls FinOps "an operational framework and cultural practice which maximizes the business value of technology", in which "everyone takes ownership of their cost and usage supported by a central best-practices group". At the Rinsemoor, nobody did.

asked: Estimate the monthly cost of this design.
When is serverless dearer than a long-running server?
What is cost per unit, and why watch it?
interview.answer: I'd estimate it as a count times a price, line by line. First, write down one unit of work's trip: for a camera frame here, 1 storage write, 2 reads and 3 hand-offs between steps. Second, price each: at $5, $0.40 and $25 per million, that's $80.80 per million frames. Third, count the units: 4 cameras at 30 frames a second for a 30-day month is 311,040,000 frames, so $25,132.03 a month; recording only during 1,200 three-minute washes is 6,480,000 frames, $523.58. Serverless gets dearer than a server that stays on when the work is a steady stream: per-request prices are tiny, but a constant flow multiplies them by a huge count, while a server costs a flat amount whatever passes through it. Below the break-even count, per-request wins; above it, the always-on server does, and keeping data in memory instead of passing it through storage removes whole lines of the bill. Cost per unit is the bill divided by what the business sells: here $20.94 a wash against $0.44 before. I'd watch it because a total can grow with good news, more customers, while cost per unit only jumps when the design or a setting has changed. With it go a budget alarm and an owner for each line of the bill. I'd tell the story of a car wash whose camera update made it pay $25,132.03 to film empty bays, and of Prime Video, which cut its monitoring tool's cost by over 90% by moving frames into memory in one process.

The built-in software inside a device such as a camera. Its updates download, install and restart the camera; the one on 1 September reset every setting.
The value a setting has until someone changes it. The cameras' default is always record.

The FinOps Foundation's name for treating the cloud bill as part of the design, with costs that everyone can see and every team owns.

A computer in the cloud company's building rented by the month that stays on, here for one bay program. A server is a computer that runs programs for others.

One of the places in the world where a cloud company keeps its computers. Prices can differ a little between regions (s1e10).

The part of a system that decides which step runs next and hands the work on. Prime Video's ran on AWS Step Functions.

AWS Step Functions' name for one move from one step to the next: the story's hand-off. $0.000025 each in US East, $25 per million.
An amount of use AWS gives free each month before charging, such as 4,000 Step Functions state transitions.

Other S3 requests: COPY makes a copy of a stored file, POST is another way to save one, and LIST asks for the names of the files in a bucket.

The small staffed booth beside the bays with a till and the shop computer, where the night attendant sits.
A kind of S3 storage built for tables of data, priced on the same page. Its example gives the PUT price the story uses.
A small separate program that does one part of a system and talks to the others over the network.
One program that does all the parts of a system together, so parts pass data in memory instead of over the network.
One running program on a computer, with its own memory. Prime Video moved every part into one process.
AWS's budget alarm: you set an amount, and it emails or messages you when spending passes or is forecast to pass it. Its figures update up to three times a day.
In the cold case, a cloud service that reads a car's number plate from a picture, charged per picture: $1 per 1,000 in this story.
An international standard for running information security. Its Annex A lists controls, among them A.5.23 on using cloud services.
The control on information security for use of cloud services: how a company takes on, uses, manages and leaves cloud services.

atWork: Look for any pipeline where each item makes a trip through paid steps: a function per upload, a step per message, a storage write per picture. Then ask who or what sets how many items there are. A per-request pipeline whose request count is set by a device or a setting, a camera's frame rate, a sensor's report interval, a phone app's refresh, a retry rule, is a common pattern, and it stays cheap only until that setting changes. For each one: write down one item's trip and its price, multiply by today's count, and divide by your business unit (per order, per customer, per wash). Put that cost per unit somewhere a named person reads it every week. Set a budget alarm, such as an AWS Budgets cost budget with an email notification, a little above the expected month, and remember it can arrive hours late. In AWS Cost Explorer, group the bill by service and usage type to see which line is a count of requests. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the nearest control is Annex A 5.23, which ISMS.online says "outlines the processes that are required for the acquisition, use, management of and exit from cloud services"; an auditor would look at how your cloud use is managed and monitored, not at the size of the bill, so treat this as governance of cloud use, not a cost control, and build the owners and alarms into the design from the first draft.

recall.prompt: Your team runs photo booths in shopping centres. Each booth sends every picture through four serverless steps that hand the job on, saving and re-fetching the picture between steps. A booth software update turns on a live preview that sends 10 pictures a second to the same steps, even when nobody is in the booth. The month's cloud bill is 60 times the usual. What happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The bill is a count times a price per request, and the count was set by the booth's setting, not by customers
Do the steady work in one program that stays on, keeps pictures in memory and saves only what is needed
Watch cost per unit (per photo session) with a named owner for each line of the bill

recall.model: The bill is a count times a price per request: every preview picture made four trips, with saves, re-fetches and hand-offs, and the count was set by the booth's new setting, not by customers, so empty booths ran up the bill all day. Turning the preview off brings the count back, but the design still pays per picture. I'd move each booth's work into one program that stays on, keeps the preview in memory and saves only the photos a customer buys, so paid requests follow sessions. Then I'd put cost per session on a weekly sheet with a named owner for each line of the bill, and a budget alert a little above the expected month.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with everything else as built, which one change alone brings September's bill under $100?
options: Record only when a car is in the bay
One program per bay, saving 2 photos a wash
recall.why: One program per bay gives $48.01: $48.00 for the four programs and $0.01 for 2,400 photo writes, whatever the cameras record. Recording only with a car gives $523.58. The discount gives $21,362.23, and keeping footage 7 days leaves the bill at $25,132.03, because the bill counts requests, not space.

recall.prompt: A storage write costs $5 per million, a read $0.40 per million and a hand-off $25 per million. One frame is 1 write, 2 reads and 3 hand-offs. What do a million frames cost?
recall.why: 1 x $5 + 2 x $0.40 + 3 x $25 = $5 + $0.80 + $75 = $80.80 per million frames. $30.40 counts one of each; $55.80 counts two hand-offs; $75.80 leaves out the write. The hand-offs are most of it.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: when is serverless dearer than a long-running server, and how would you know before the bill tells you?

keyIdeas.idea: Serverless charges per request, so a steady, high-volume stream multiplies a tiny price by a huge count
A server that stays on costs a flat amount however much passes through it, so above a break-even count it is cheaper
Estimate count times price before building, and watch cost per business unit after

recall.model: Serverless charges per request, which is cheap when work comes in bursts with long gaps. It gets dearer when the work is a steady, high-volume stream: a tiny price times a huge count, such as 30 camera frames a second all month. A server that stays on costs a flat amount however much passes through it, so above a break-even count it is cheaper, especially if keeping data in memory removes storage writes and hand-offs too. I'd know before the bill by estimating: write down one unit's trip, price each request, multiply by the expected count, and compare that with the flat price. After launch I'd watch cost per unit, per order or per wash, with a named owner and a budget alarm.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The bay programs have run since Monday 5 October; November's bill was $48.01 for 1,200 washes. On Tuesday 1 December Mrs Oluwole turned on plate reading for a new loyalty card: each bay program sends pictures to the cloud company's plate reader, $1 per 1,000 pictures in this story's prices. The contractor wired it to the frames the program already holds, so while a car is in the bay, they all go to the reader. That evening the budget alarm, still at $100, emailed her, and she switched plate reading off at 08:00 on Wednesday 2 December. Tuesday's 40 washes cost $216.00 in plate reading alone.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did one day of plate reading cost $216.00, and how should it be built?

keyIdeas.idea: The reader charges per picture and the count was set by the frame rate: thirty a second for the whole of every wash
Read the plate once per wash: one picture, sent when the car sensor says the car is in place
The alarm worked because someone owned it; work out the cost per wash of any new feature before it goes live

coldCase.model: It is September's mistake in miniature. The plate reader charges per picture, and the count was set by the frame rate, not by the washes: every frame of every wash went to it, thirty a second for 3 minutes, 5,400 pictures a wash, $5.40 a wash, and 216,000 pictures, $216.00, for Tuesday's 40 washes. Read the plate once per wash: one picture, sent when the car sensor says the car is in place, 40 pictures a day, $0.04. The alarm worked because Mrs Oluwole owns the bill now and acted the next morning. Next time, work out the cost per wash of a new feature before it goes live: one wash's requests times the price.
